Free Printable Plant Propagation Tracker (PDF)

This is a free, one-page printable plant propagation tracker in PDF format. Each row is one batch of cuttings: the date started, the parent plant, the method (water, soil, sphagnum moss, division, leaf), how many you took, the date you first saw roots, the date you potted them up, and notes on what worked. Propagation is slow enough that you forget when you started and fast enough that cuttings rot if you forget them — a dated log fixes both, and after a few batches it tells you which method actually works in your home.

Method notes

Water propagation is the easiest to watch and the best for learning: you see the roots form. Its weakness is that water roots are fragile and some cuttings sulk when moved to soil — pot up when roots are an inch or two long, not longer, and keep the soil moist for the first couple of weeks. Soil propagation skips that transition but hides the progress; a gentle tug that meets resistance after a few weeks means roots. Sphagnum moss or perlite sits between the two and suits aroids that rot in water.

Whatever the method, a cutting needs a node — the bump on the stem where a leaf or aerial root emerges — for most vining plants. Leaf-only cuttings of pothos or monstera grow roots but never a new plant. Succulent leaves are the exception and root from the leaf base.

  • Take cuttings in spring or summer; rooting slows dramatically in short winter days.
  • Bright indirect light and warmth around 70°F (21°C) speed everything up; cold windowsills stall it.
  • Change propagation water every few days, and discard any cutting whose stem turns brown and soft.

Typical rooting times

Rough expectations for the Roots seen column under warm, bright indoor conditions. Cold, dim, or winter conditions can double these.

PlantEasiest methodRoots usually appearNotes
Pothos, heartleaf philodendronWater1–3 weeksNeeds a node; very forgiving
Monstera deliciosaWater or moss3–6 weeksInclude a node and, ideally, an aerial root
Spider plant plantletsWater or straight into soil1–2 weeksOften already has root nubs
TradescantiaWater or soil1–2 weeksRoots from any node
Succulent leaves (echeveria, jade)Dry callus, then on top of soil2–6 weeks for roots; months for a rosetteDo not bury the leaf; mist lightly
Snake plant leaf sectionsWater or soil4–8 weeks or longerKeep the cut end that was lower on the leaf pointing down
String of pearlsLaid on soil2–4 weeksPin the strand to the surface
ZZ plant leafSoil2–4 monthsForms a rhizome first; very slow
African violet, begonia leafSoil or water4–8 weeksNew plantlets appear at the leaf base
Peace lily, ferns, calatheaDivision when repottingAlready rootedNot from cuttings; split the root ball

Ranges are typical, not guaranteed. Log your own dates — your conditions will shift them, and the sheet becomes the better reference.

How to use this sheet

  1. Print the PDF and keep it beside the propagation jars or shelf.
  2. Each batch of cuttings gets one row: date, parent plant, method, and how many cuttings — a label on the jar with the same date helps.
  3. Check weekly. Write the date you first see roots, and note anything that failed and why (rot, dried out, no node).
  4. When roots are an inch or two long, pot up and record the date. Keep the soil evenly moist for the first two weeks.
  5. After a few batches, compare dates by method — that tells you which method to use next time for each plant.

Questions

Is this sheet really free?

Yes. The PDF is free to download and print — no sign-up, no email, no watermark.

How long do cuttings take to root?

One to three weeks for easy vines like pothos in water, three to six for monstera, and one to three months for slow plants like snake plant and ZZ. Warmth and bright indirect light are the biggest accelerators; the table above lists common plants.

Why are my cuttings rotting instead of rooting?

Usually too little light, too cold, water left unchanged, or a cutting without a node. Discard anything soft and brown, cut the stem back to healthy tissue, and start again in fresh water with more light.

Can I propagate in winter?

You can, but expect it to take much longer and lose more cuttings. If you can, wait for spring — or put the cuttings under a grow light to compensate for short days.
